You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Sign

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, a 'sign' (Hebrew 'oth; Greek semeion) is understood as a divinely given event, act, or object that points beyond itself to God's presence, power, and purpose — an attesting pointer that authenticates God's revelation, covenant, or messenger. In the Gospel of John especially, 'signs' are Jesus' miracles understood not as ends in themselves but as revelations of his identity and glory, intended to lead observers to faith. More broadly, a sign functions as a symbol of divine attestation: it confirms a promise (covenant signs), validates a prophet or apostle, or discloses a coming reality (eschatological signs).",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 2:11 (the first sign at Cana revealing Jesus' glory)",
    "John 20:30-31 (signs written 'that you may believe')",
    "Exodus 4:8-9; 7:3 (signs authenticating Moses before Pharaoh)",
    "Isaiah 7:14 (the sign of Immanuel)",
    "Genesis 9:12-13 (rainbow as sign of the covenant)",
    "Genesis 17:11 (circumcision as sign of the covenant)",
    "Exodus 31:13 (Sabbath as a sign between God and Israel)",
    "Matthew 12:39-40 (the sign of Jonah pointing to the resurrection)",
    "Luke 2:12 (the sign given to the shepherds)",
    "2 Corinthians 12:12 (signs of a true apostle)",
    "Hebrews 2:4 (God bearing witness by signs and wonders)",
    "Genesis 1:14 (heavenly lights 'for signs and seasons')"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Covenant sign and seal: signs (rainbow, circumcision, Sabbath, and by extension baptism and the Lord's Supper) as visible marks and seals of God's covenant promises — the sacramental reading emphasized in Reformed and Catholic theology.",

        "Genesis 9:12-17",
        "Genesis 17:11",
        "Exodus 31:13,17",
        "Romans 4:11 (circumcision as 'a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith')"
      ],

    },
    {
      "meaning": "Eschatological portent: signs as heavenly or historical omens announcing the end times, the day of the Lord, or Christ's return ('signs of the times').",

        "Matthew 16:3",

        "Luke 21:11,25",
        "Joel 2:30-31 / Acts 2:19",
        "Revelation 12:1-3; 15:1"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Authenticating miracle: signs primarily as wonders that validate a divinely commissioned messenger (Moses, the prophets, Jesus, the apostles), with emphasis on the miracle's evidential function.",

        "Exodus 4:1-9",
        "John 3:2 (Nicodemus: 'no one can do these signs unless God is with him')",
        "Acts 2:22",

      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Negative or judgment-oriented reading: sign-seeking as a mark of unbelief, and signs (including the sign of Jonah) read as warnings of judgment on an unrepentant generation; also deceptive signs performed by false christs and the man of lawlessness.",

        "Matthew 12:38-39; 16:4 ('an evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign')",
        "1 Corinthians 1:22 ('Jews demand signs')",
        "Matthew 24:24 (false christs performing great signs)",
        "2 Thessalonians 2:9 (lying signs and wonders)",
        "Revelation 13:13-14; 16:14; 19:20 (signs performed by the beast/false prophet)"

      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Prophetic sign-act: symbolic actions performed by prophets (and their children or bodies) as living signs dramatizing God's message, e.g., Isaiah's children, Ezekiel's enacted parables.",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 8:18 ('I and the children the LORD has given me are signs')",
        "Isaiah 20:3",
        "Ezekiel 4:1-3; 12:6,11; 24:24,27"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is broad, recognizable consensus that 'sign' in Scripture denotes a pointer beyond itself to divine reality — an attesting, revelatory, or covenantal marker rather than a mere marvel. The main interpretive divergences concern emphasis rather than substance: Johannine scholarship stresses signs as christological revelation eliciting faith; sacramental traditions stress covenant signs and seals; apocalyptic and popular prophecy traditions stress eschatological portents; and a corrective strand highlights the biblical critique of sign-seeking and warnings about deceptive signs. Because 'sign' is a broad, multi-context term rather than a single symbol, the consensus is about its function (divine attestation and pointing) rather than a single fixed referent."
}

Its referent depends on context: miracle, covenant marker, prophetic token, eschatological omen, sacramental element, or deceptive wonder."

No major Christian tradition redefines the term outside this family of meanings."

BOOK ENTRY
A prophecy given in advance — often a prophet's lived story — whose fulfillment testifies; not a wonder performed on demand.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: a miraculous act pointing to God's power and Christ's identity.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Isa 7:14; Ezek 24:24; Luke 11:30) · see Signs and Similitudes, ch. 3

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Isaiah 7:14 — Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
Ezekiel 24:24 — Thus Ezekiel is unto you a sign: according to all that he hath done shall ye do: and when this cometh, ye shall know that I am the Lord GOD.
Luke 11:30 — For as Jonas was a sign unto the Ninevites, so shall also the Son of man be to this generation.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
